title: Navy wants its own AI-piloted drone fighters to put on aircraft carriers
key_facts: The US Navy wants its own carrier-based AI-piloted drone fighters, called collaborative combat aircraft (CCAs).

Per USNI News, the Navy request for information, which closed on 18 Sep, asks for two prototypes that can first fly within two years and reach shore-based carrier certification within three years of contract award.
The drones must operate from Nimitz- and Ford-class carriers and also from rough airstrips.
They must carry at least four 2,500-pound munitions underwing, implying a 10,000-pound payload.
The Navy is reportedly aiming for a combat radius of about 1,000 nautical miles, with up to 30 minutes of loiter.
The target price is under $30 million per aircraft, roughly one-third the price of a carrier-based F-35C.
The Air Force already has two CCAs in production: Anduril's FQ-44 Fury and General Atomics' FQ-42 Vengeance.
quote_evidence: The U.S. Navy is looking to field its own carrier-based AI-piloted drone fighters, and now we finally have an idea of what it wants these jets to do, and how much they want them to cost.

Per reporting from USNI News, the Navy RFI, which closed on September 18, says the branch wants two fully functional drone fighter prototypes that can achieve first flight within two years and shore-based carrier certification within three years, or optimally less, of contract award.
The Navy wants them to cost in at under $30 million per aircraft, or roughly one-third the price of a carrier-based F-35C.
why_it_matters_hint: The Navy's requirements show what a carrier-launched AI-piloted warplane would need to do and cost.
notes: A request for information is not a contract; details come via USNI News.
